topic.title: Behavioral, HR & Interview Strategy
topic.summary: The questions that decide close calls: tell me about yourself, STAR stories, strengths and weaknesses, conflicts, failures, salary, and a repeatable routine for live coding rounds.
topic.overview:
## Why this topic matters
Technical skill gets you shortlisted; communication, ownership and attitude often decide the offer. For junior roles in particular, interviewers hire for **potential**: can you learn, work with a team, take feedback and own your mistakes?

## Typical interview process
Details differ by company, but a common sequence in Bangladesh and abroad is:
1. **Online assessment or written test** (coding problems, sometimes MCQs on CS fundamentals; banks and some large companies may also have aptitude tests).
2. **Technical interviews** (DSA, CS fundamentals, your projects and the stack on your CV).
3. **HR / culture round** (motivation, behaviour, salary, joining date).
Behavioral questions appear in *almost every* round: "tell me about yourself" and "tell me about your project" open most technical interviews.

## What interviewers listen for
- **Ownership**: "I" for your actions, honest about mistakes.
- **Evidence**: stories and numbers instead of adjectives.
- **Communication**: structured, concise answers (STAR).
- **Learning**: what you changed after a failure or feedback.
- **Fit**: genuine, researched interest in this company and role.

## How to prepare
1. Build a **story bank** of 5-6 STAR stories (challenge, conflict, failure, leadership, learning fast, pressure). Each story can answer several questions.
2. Write and rehearse your **present-past-future** introduction for each type of company you apply to.
3. Practise **out loud**, with a timer, in English (most software interviews use English or a mix with Bangla). Clarity beats accent.
4. Research every company and prepare **questions to ask**.
5. Rehearse the **coding-interview routine** until thinking aloud feels natural.

questions.title: Tell me about yourself
questions.prompt:
"So, tell me about yourself."

It is usually the very first question, in HR rounds *and* technical rounds. How do you answer it as a fresh graduate, and what should a strong 60-90 second answer contain?
hints: They are not asking for your life story. They want a short pitch that shows why you are relevant to this job.
Use a simple structure: present -> past -> future.
Present: who you are and your focus. Past: 2-3 proof points (project, internship, achievement) with a number. Future: why this role is your natural next step.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Starts with hometown, school and family, lists every course and hobby, talks for four minutes, and ends with "...so yeah, that's me."

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: A rehearsed (not memorised) 60-90 second present-past-future pitch with two or three concrete proof points that match the job description, ending with why this role, then handing the conversation back.

solution.summary: Answer in 60-90 seconds using present, past, future: who you are now, two or three concrete proof points from projects or internships, and why this role is the logical next step, all tailored to the job description.
solution.explanation:
### Why they ask
It is a warm-up, but it also sets the agenda: interviewers often pick their next question from something you mention. So mention things you **want** to be asked about.

### The present-past-future template
1. **Present (1-2 sentences)**: degree, what you enjoy building, your main stack.
2. **Past (2-3 proof points)**: your best project, an internship or part-time job, one extra achievement. For each: what *you* did plus a result or number.
3. **Future (1-2 sentences)**: what you want next and why this role/company fits.

### Sample answer for a fresh graduate (about 150 words, roughly a minute spoken)
> I'm a Computer Science graduate from [University], and I enjoy building web applications end to end, mostly with Next.js, Node.js and MongoDB.
>
> For my final-year project I led a team of three building a bus-ticket booking system. I designed the REST API and the seat-reservation logic so two people can never book the same seat, and about 200 classmates used it during testing. I also did a three-month internship at a fintech startup, where I wrote integration tests for their payment APIs and found a bug that was sending duplicate receipts. I've also solved around 300 problems on LeetCode and Codeforces to sharpen my problem solving.
>
> Now I'm looking for a backend-focused role where I can work on real production systems, and this position on your payments team is exactly that, which is why I applied. I'm happy to go deeper into any of these.

Replace the details with your own, and keep every claim something you can discuss for five minutes.

### Tips
- **Tailor it**: pick proof points that match 2-3 lines of the job description. A bank IT role and a startup frontend role deserve different versions.
- **Leave out**: age, marital status, family details, every course you took, your full CGPA history (one line is enough if it is strong).
- **No CV recital**: they have your CV; tell the story behind it.
- **Practise out loud** until it sounds natural; memorise the structure and key facts, not every word.
- **Language**: many software interviews are in English or a mix of English and Bangla. Prepare it in English; clarity matters far more than accent.
- **Time it**: under 90 seconds. If they want more, they will ask.
keyPoints: Present -> past -> future in 60-90 seconds
Two or three concrete proof points with what YOU did and a result
Tailored to the job description, not a recital of the CV
Ends with why this role, then hands the conversation back
Plant topics you are happy to be asked about

visuals.title: A one-minute answer, built piece by piece
visuals.caption: Lanes are the three parts of the template; the axis is seconds of speaking time at a calm pace (about 130 words per minute).

steps.note: **Present (about 10 s).** Who you are now and what you focus on: *"I'm a Computer Science graduate from [University], and I enjoy building web applications end to end, mostly with Next.js, Node.js and MongoDB."*

**Past, proof 1: your best project (about 20 s).** One sentence of context, what *you* did, one number: *"For my final-year project I led a team of three building a bus-ticket booking system. I designed the REST API and the seat-reservation logic so two people can never book the same seat, and about 200 classmates used it during testing."*

**Past, proof 2: internship or job (about 13 s).** *"I also did a three-month internship at a fintech startup, where I wrote integration tests for their payment APIs and found a bug that was sending duplicate receipts."*

**Past, proof 3: something extra (a few seconds).** Contests, open source, teaching assistant work: *"I've also solved around 300 problems on LeetCode and Codeforces."* Skip it if you have nothing strong.

**Future (about 12 s).** Connect your story to *this* role: *"Now I'm looking for a backend-focused role where I can work on real production systems, and this position on your payments team is exactly that."*

**End cleanly** and hand the conversation back: *"That's a quick overview. I'm happy to go deeper into any of these."* Total: about 140-150 words, a little over a minute at a calm pace, which leaves room for one more detail while staying under 90 seconds.

followUps.question: What do you do outside of coding?
followUps.answer: One or two genuine interests, briefly, ideally showing a quality such as discipline (sport), teaching (tutoring), or curiosity (reading). Keep it short and honest.

followUps.question: Why did you choose computer science?
followUps.answer: A short, true story: the moment you first built something that worked, and what keeps you interested now. Connect it to the kind of work this role involves.

questions.title: Walk me through your resume and projects
questions.prompt:
"Walk me through your resume." / "Tell me about a project you are proud of."

How do you present your CV and your projects so the interviewer sees real engineering depth, and how do you prepare for the follow-up questions that every line of your CV invites?
hints: They already read the CV. What do they want that the CV cannot show?
For a project: problem, your role, architecture, hardest part, result, what you would improve.
Assume every line can be drilled three levels deep. Anything you cannot defend for five minutes should not be on the CV.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Reads the CV top to bottom, describes projects as feature lists ("it has login, search and booking"), says "we" throughout, and has no answer when asked "why MongoDB?" or "what was the hardest bug?".

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Gives a 2-minute guided tour that ends with the best project, then walks through that project as a story: problem, own role, architecture with reasons, hardest technical problem and how it was solved, measurable result, and honest improvements.

solution.summary: Give a two-minute guided tour of the CV (education in one line, experience, best projects, extras, why this role), then present your strongest project as an engineering story: the problem, what you personally built, the architecture and why, the hardest bug or decision, the result, and what you would improve.
solution.explanation:
### Part 1: the 2-minute tour
Go in an order that builds to your strongest material:
1. **Education** in one line (degree, focus, a strong CGPA or thesis if relevant).
2. **Experience**: internship or part-time work, with what you shipped.
3. **Best project(s)**: one or two, briefly.
4. **Extras**: contests, open source, teaching assistant, hackathons.
5. **Bridge**: why this role is the next step.

### Part 2: the project deep dive (the part that decides the interview)
Use this ladder; each rung is a question they will ask anyway:
1. **Problem and users**: who needed it and why.
2. **Your role**: what *you* built. Say "I" for your work and "we" for the team's.
3. **Architecture**: stack, data model, main flows, and **why** you chose them (and what you would choose today).
4. **Hardest part**: one bug or decision in detail. Example: *"During testing two users booked the same seat. I reproduced it with a script that sent 50 parallel requests, found a check-then-insert race, and replaced it with a single atomic update that only succeeds if the seat is still free, plus a unique index on (trip, seat)."*
5. **Result**: users, performance numbers, grade, demo, deployment.
6. **Next time**: honest improvements (tests, caching, better schema). This shows maturity.

### Prepare three levels down
"Why MongoDB?" -> "How did you model bookings?" -> "What happens with two concurrent bookings?" -> "How would it handle 100x users?" If you cannot go three levels deep on a topic, either study it or remove it from the CV.

### Common traps for freshers
- **Buzzword skills**: listing Kubernetes, Kafka or machine learning after one tutorial. Interviewers pick exactly these lines.
- **Group projects** where you cannot explain the parts you did not build. Know the whole system at a high level and your part in depth.
- **No numbers**: "fast", "many users". Measure something: response time, users, test coverage, problems solved.
- **Badmouthing** a teammate, a university or a previous employer.

Project story: problem, your role, architecture and why, hardest part, result, improvements
Say "I" for your contribution; know the whole system at a high level
Every CV line must survive three levels of follow-up questions
Use numbers and one concrete technical story

questions.title: Why should we hire you?
questions.prompt:
"Why should we hire you?" or "What makes you a good fit for this role?"

Fresh graduates often freeze here or answer with adjectives. How do you build a convincing answer?
hints: Answer from their side: what problem are they hiring to solve?
Match the job description's top requirements with evidence from your projects, internship and studies.
Three reasons, each with proof, then a one-line close about the value you bring. 45-60 seconds.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "I am hard-working, passionate and a quick learner." Every candidate says this; there is no proof and no link to the role.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Maps the top requirements of the job description to concrete evidence, picks the three strongest matches, adds one proof of fast learning, and closes with the value to the team, in under a minute and without putting other candidates down.

solution.summary: Pick the three requirements of the job that you match best and prove each one with something you actually built or did, add evidence that you learn quickly, and close with the value you will bring to their team, in under a minute.
solution.explanation:
### What they are really asking
"Can you summarise, with evidence, why you fit *this* job?" It tests self-awareness, preparation and communication.

### Build it from the job description (see the visual)
1. List the 5-6 key requirements from the job description.
2. Write your evidence for each: a project, internship task, course project, contest, or teaching experience.
3. Choose the **three strongest matches** for this role.
4. Add one sign that you **learn fast** (juniors are hired for potential).
5. Close with value: what you can contribute and how quickly.

### Sample answer (junior backend role at a payments company)
> You are looking for someone who can build reliable backend services. In my final-year project I built a 20-endpoint Express API with authentication, and I found and fixed a concurrency bug where two users could book the same seat. During my internship I learned PostgreSQL on the job and was writing production reports within three weeks, so I pick things up quickly. And I am genuinely interested in payments: I built a small wallet app to understand how to make transfers idempotent. So I can contribute to your API work early, and where I don't know something yet, I'll learn it fast.

### Variations
- **Service company**: emphasise adaptability (different stacks per client), communication with clients, delivering on deadlines.
- **Bank / fintech IT**: emphasise reliability, attention to detail, SQL, and respect for process and security.
- **Startup**: emphasise ownership, speed, and building end to end.

### Do not
- Compare yourself with other candidates ("I'm better than the others").
- Sound desperate ("I really need this job").
- Use only adjectives.
keyPoints: Answer from the employer's side: the problem they are hiring for
Three requirement -> evidence matches, chosen for this specific role
Proof that you learn fast
Close with the value you bring; 45-60 seconds

questions.title: Why do you want to join this company?
questions.prompt:
"Why do you want to work here?" or "What do you know about our company?"

How do you research a company and turn that research into an answer that sounds specific and genuine, whether it is a product company, a software service company, a bank or a startup?
hints: If your answer would work for any other company, it is too generic.
Find something specific about the product or mission, the engineering work, and the role itself.
Formula: company (a specific thing you admire) + role (what you will do and learn) + you (why your background fits).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "It is a big, well-known company with a good salary and work environment." Nothing specific, and it is about what you get, not what you bring.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Mentions one specific, researched thing about the company (product, customers, engineering practice), connects it to the role and team, and links it to your own background and goals in 45-60 seconds.

solution.summary: Show that you researched them: name one specific thing about their product or mission, one about their engineering or the role, and connect both to your own skills and goals, so the answer could only be about this company.
solution.explanation:
### What they are testing
Interest (are you likely to accept and stay?), preparation, and whether your goals match what the job really is.

### Research in 30-60 minutes
- **Use the product** (install the app, try the website) and read some user reviews.
- **Website**: products, customers, markets, recent news.
- **Engineering signals**: engineering blog, GitHub, conference talks, job posts (which stack, which teams), LinkedIn posts by their engineers.
- **People**: seniors or alumni who work there; ask what the work is really like.
- **The job description**: which team, which systems, what they emphasise.

### The formula: company + role + you
> **Company**: "I've used your app for two years, and what stands out is how reliably payments go through even during festival rush hours. I'd love to understand how that is engineered."
> **Role**: "This role is on the backend payments team, so I would be working on exactly those reliability problems, with code reviews and mentoring from experienced engineers."
> **You**: "In my final-year project and a small wallet side project I worked on idempotent transactions and concurrency, so this is the direction I want to grow in."

(The company details here are placeholders: use real, specific facts from your own research.)

### Tailor by company type
See the comparison visual. A service company values adaptability and client work; a bank values reliability and process; a startup values ownership and speed.

### Avoid
- Only salary, location, brand name or "work-life balance" as reasons.
- Facts you cannot back up, or copying the "About us" page word for word.
- Saying it is your "backup option" or that you applied everywhere.

pitfalls: A generic answer that would fit any company
Focusing only on salary, perks or the brand name
Getting basic facts about the company wrong
Overpraising in a way that sounds memorised

followUps.question: What do you know about our products?
followUps.answer: Name the main products or services, who uses them, and one thing you noticed while using one. If you could not try it (internal banking systems, for example), mention what you learned from the website, news or people who work there.

followUps.question: Which other companies are you interviewing with?
followUps.answer: Be honest but brief and non-specific: "I am talking to a couple of other companies, mostly backend roles, but this role is my priority because..." Do not list names or play companies against each other at this stage.

questions.title: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
questions.prompt:
"What is your greatest strength?" and "What is your biggest weakness?"

How do you choose a strength worth mentioning, and how do you talk about a real weakness honestly without hurting your chances?
hints: A strength without an example is just a claim.
The weakness question tests self-awareness and growth, not perfection. Clichés like "I am a perfectionist" fail that test.
Weakness formula: a real but non-critical weakness, a moment it hurt, what you changed, and evidence it is improving.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Strength: "I am hard-working." Weakness: "I am a perfectionist" or "I work too hard", or worse, a weakness that is central to the job.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Strength: one or two qualities relevant to the role, each with a short story. Weakness: a real, non-core weakness, a specific example of its impact, the concrete system used to improve, and measurable progress.

solution.summary: For strengths, pick one or two that matter for the role and prove each with a short example. For the weakness, choose a real but non-critical one, show a moment it hurt, explain the concrete steps you took to improve, and give evidence that it is getting better.
solution.explanation:
### Strengths: claim + proof + relevance
> "One of my strengths is debugging methodically. During my internship, a payment receipt was being emailed twice. Instead of guessing, I reproduced it in a test, traced it to a retry that was not idempotent, and fixed it with a unique event id. For a backend role, I think that habit matters a lot."

Good junior strengths: learning fast, debugging, ownership, communication, consistency (e.g. daily problem solving), teaching others. Choose ones you can prove.

### Weaknesses: the four-part formula (see the timeline)
1. **A real weakness** that is not core to the job.
2. **A moment it hurt** (shows honesty and self-awareness).
3. **What you changed**: a concrete system, not "I will try harder".
4. **Evidence of progress**.

### Good weakness topics for a fresh graduate
- Underestimating tasks (as in the visual).
- Hesitating to ask for help and losing time when stuck; fix: a time box (e.g. ask after an hour of being stuck, with what you tried).
- Nervousness in public speaking; fix: volunteering to present demos, joining a club.
- A technical gap that is honest and fixable: "I have not deployed to a cloud provider in production yet; I am deploying my side project with Docker on a VPS to learn."

### Weaknesses to avoid
- Clichés ("perfectionist", "I work too hard").
- "I have no weaknesses."
- Weaknesses that are core to the role ("I don't like working in teams" for a team role, "I am careless with details" for a banking system).
keyPoints: Strength = relevant quality + short proof story
Weakness = real, non-core, with an example of its impact
Show a concrete improvement system and evidence of progress
Avoid clichés and weaknesses that are central to the role

visuals.title: A weakness answer that shows growth
visuals.caption: Example weakness: underestimating tasks. The axis is weeks.

steps.note: **The real weakness, with a moment it hurt**: *"I used to underestimate tasks. In my final-year project I said the payment integration would take three days; it took two weeks, and our demo slipped by a week."*
**Action 1**: *"Now I break every task into pieces of less than a day before I give an estimate,"* which exposes the unknown parts early.
**Action 2**: *"I log my estimate next to the actual time for each task,"* so the estimates get calibrated by data, not optimism.
**Action 3**: *"If something is going over by day two, I tell the team immediately instead of hoping to catch up."*

**Evidence it is improving**: *"During the last two months of my internship my estimates were within about 20% of the actual time, and I have not missed a deadline since."* Real weakness, concrete system, measurable progress.

rows: Cliché; sounds rehearsed and dodges the question
"I am not good at working in teams."
Core to almost every engineering job
"I used to underestimate tasks; now I split and track them."
Real, common, fixable, with a concrete system
"I hesitated to ask for help; now I ask after an hour, with what I tried."
Honest and shows good team habits
"I have not used a cloud provider in production; I am deploying my project to learn."
Honest skill gap plus an active plan

pitfalls: Using "perfectionist" or "I work too hard" as a weakness
Naming a weakness that disqualifies you for the role
Describing the weakness but no concrete improvement
Claiming strengths without any example

followUps.question: What would your previous manager or supervisor say you need to improve?
followUps.answer: Use real feedback you received and what you did with it: "My internship lead said I should ask questions earlier. I started posting what I had tried after an hour of being stuck, and it saved me a lot of time."

followUps.question: Give me another weakness.
followUps.answer: Prepare a second one in the same format, ideally a technical gap with a learning plan, so you are not caught off guard.

questions.title: Tell me about your most challenging project (STAR method)
questions.prompt:
"Tell me about the most challenging project you have worked on."

Answer it with the **STAR** method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). What makes a STAR story strong, how long should each part be, and what does a good technical example from a fresh graduate sound like?
hints: Choose a story where the challenge was real and *you* made the difference.
STAR: Situation (context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what you did), Result (outcome and lesson).
Spend most of the time on Action, say "I", include technical detail, and end with a number and a lesson.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Our final-year project was very challenging because we had little time, but we worked hard as a team and finished it." No specific problem, no personal actions, no result.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: A focused STAR story about one hard problem: brief situation, clear personal responsibility and stakes, step-by-step actions with technical reasoning, a measurable result and a lesson, in about two minutes.

solution.summary: Use STAR in about two minutes: one or two sentences of situation, your specific task and the stakes, then most of the time on the concrete actions you personally took and why, finishing with a measurable result and what you learned.
solution.explanation:
### STAR in one line each
- **Situation**: the context, briefly (where, when, what was happening).
- **Task**: what **you** were responsible for and why it was hard or important.
- **Action**: the steps **you** took, in order, with your reasoning. This is 50-60% of the answer.
- **Result**: the outcome, with numbers if possible, plus one lesson.

### Picking the story
- A real technical challenge (a hard bug, performance problem, learning a new technology under a deadline) beats "we had little time".
- You must have played a central role.
- It should be recent and relevant to the job.
- Have a second story ready in case they say "something else, please".

### Full sample answer (the visual walks through it piece by piece)
> **Situation**: In my final-year project, a bus-ticket booking web app, we invited about 200 classmates to test it a week before our final demo.
> **Task**: I owned the booking API. During testing two students got tickets for the same seat, and I had a week to fix it.
> **Action**: First I reproduced it: I wrote a script that sent 50 booking requests for the same seat at the same moment, and it double-booked in most runs. The code checked whether the seat was free and then inserted the booking, so two requests could both pass the check. I replaced it with one atomic update that only succeeds if the seat is still available, and added a unique index on trip and seat as a safety net. I re-ran the script 20 times, turned it into an automated test, and explained the pattern to my teammates so they checked the payment flow too.
> **Result**: Zero double bookings in 1,000 concurrent attempts, a smooth demo, and one of the top grades in our batch. I learned to think about concurrency whenever two users can touch the same data, and to always reproduce a bug before fixing it.

### Build a story bank
Prepare 5-6 STAR stories (challenge, conflict, failure, leadership, learning something fast, pressure). Each story can answer several questions with a different emphasis.
keyPoints: STAR: short situation and task, long action, measurable result
Say "I" and explain your reasoning, not just the steps
Choose a real technical challenge where you made the difference
End with a number and a lesson; about two minutes total
Keep a bank of 5-6 stories for different questions

visuals.title: A STAR answer in under two minutes
visuals.caption: Lanes are the four STAR parts; the axis is seconds at a calm interview pace (about 115 words per minute). Notice how much of the time is Action.

steps.note: **S - Situation (1-2 sentences).** *"In my final-year project, a bus-ticket booking web app, we invited about 200 classmates to test it a week before our final demo."*
**T - Task.** What *you* owned and what was at stake: *"I owned the booking API. During testing, two students received tickets for the same seat, and I had one week to fix it before the demo."*
**A - Action, step 1: reproduce.** *"I couldn't fix what I couldn't see, so I wrote a script that sent 50 booking requests for the same seat at the same time. It double-booked in most runs."*

**A - Action, step 2: root cause and fix.** *"The code checked whether the seat was free and then inserted the booking: two requests could both pass the check. I replaced it with one atomic update that only succeeds if the seat is still available, and added a unique index on trip and seat as a safety net."*

**A - Action, step 3: verify.** *"I re-ran the script 20 times, added it as an automated test, and explained the race condition to my teammates so they checked the payment flow for the same pattern."*
**R - Result.** Numbers: *"Zero double bookings in 1,000 concurrent attempts, the demo went smoothly, and the project received one of the top grades in our batch."*

**R - Lesson.** One line: *"I learned to think about concurrency whenever two users can touch the same data, and to reproduce a bug before fixing it."* Most of the time went to **Action**, which is what the interviewer is scoring.

visuals.title: Weak vs strong STAR story
rows: One specific hard problem (a race condition before the demo)
"I" for your actions, credit to others where due
Step by step, with technical reasoning

pitfalls: Spending most of the time on the situation and background
Saying "we" so the interviewer cannot see your contribution
A result with no outcome or number
Picking a story where the challenge was only "we were busy"

followUps.question: What would you do differently?
followUps.answer: Name a real improvement: "I would write the concurrency test before building the feature, and use an atomic conditional update or a unique constraint from day one rather than a check-then-insert in application code (a plain transaction at the default isolation level does not stop this race)."

followUps.question: How did your team react?
followUps.answer: Show collaboration: "They were worried about the demo, so I shared daily progress and explained the fix in a short session, which also helped them spot a similar issue in payments."

questions.title: Tell me about a conflict with a teammate
questions.prompt:
"Tell me about a time you had a conflict or disagreement with a teammate. How did you handle it?"

What is the interviewer looking for, and how do you tell a conflict story that shows maturity rather than blame?
hints: They want to see how you behave under friction, not who was right.
Good conflict stories show: talking privately and early, understanding the other side, focusing on the shared goal, and a constructive outcome.
STAR again, with extra attention to empathy and what you learned. Never make the other person the villain.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "My teammate was lazy, so I did his part myself and told our supervisor." Blames, avoids the conversation, escalates first, and shows no learning.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: A STAR story about a real disagreement where you talked one-to-one early, listened to understand the cause, agreed on a shared goal or criteria, found a solution, and kept a good relationship, with a lesson about how you work with people.

solution.summary: Tell a short STAR story where you raised the issue privately and early, listened to understand the other person's view, moved the discussion to the shared goal and facts, agreed on a solution (escalating only if needed), and kept the working relationship good, then share what you learned.
solution.explanation:
### What they evaluate
Emotional maturity, communication, ownership and whether you can disagree without damaging the team. Engineers disagree all the time (design choices, code review, priorities); the question is how.

### A healthy conflict path (see the state diagram)
1. **Talk one-to-one, early**, not in a group chat or in front of the supervisor.
2. **Listen and ask why** before arguing. Many "conflicts" are hidden constraints.
3. **Agree on the shared goal** ("we both want a working demo on Friday").
4. **Compare options with facts** (data, a quick prototype, documentation).
5. **Decide**; if still stuck, **escalate together** to the lead with both options.
6. **Commit fully** to the decision, and **follow up**.

### Sample STAR answer
> **Situation**: In our final-year project, one teammate kept missing the deadlines for his part, the admin dashboard, and the rest of us were getting frustrated.
> **Task**: As the team lead, I needed the dashboard done for our mid-term review in two weeks without damaging the team.
> **Action**: Instead of complaining in the group chat, I asked him for a coffee and simply asked how things were going. He told me he had started a part-time tutoring job in the evenings and was embarrassed to say so. We re-split the work: he took the report generation and UI components he could build in shorter sessions, and I took the dashboard's API. We also started a 10-minute daily check-in for the whole team so problems surfaced earlier.
> **Result**: We delivered the dashboard two days early, he finished his parts, and the team was in a better mood. I learned to assume good intent and to ask before judging; many "lazy teammate" problems turn out to be hidden constraints.

### Technical disagreement variant
"In a course project we disagreed on MongoDB vs PostgreSQL. I suggested we list our access patterns and build a tiny prototype of the main query in both. The data showed relational queries mattered most, so we chose PostgreSQL, and my teammate led the schema design."

### Red flags
Blaming, "I was right and they were wrong", going to the supervisor first, choosing a story with no resolution, or claiming you have never had any conflict.
keyPoints: Raise it privately and early; listen first
Move from people to the shared goal and facts
Escalate only after trying, and together
Positive outcome and a preserved relationship
A lesson about how you work with people

visuals.title: A healthy path through a disagreement

frames.note: The states a mature answer goes through. Escalation is a fallback, not the first move.
frames.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2

  Disagreement --> PrivateTalk : talk one-to-one, early
  PrivateTalk --> Understand : listen, ask why
  Understand --> SharedGoal : agree what success means
  SharedGoal --> Options : compare options with facts

  Options --> Escalate : still stuck
  Escalate --> Agreed : lead decides with both views

rows: The other person is the villain
A reasonable person with a different view or constraint
Complain in the group chat or to the supervisor
Understand, then decide using the shared goal and facts
Frustration still visible in the telling
No resolution, or "I just did it myself"
A solution both accepted, work delivered

pitfalls: Blaming or mocking the other person
Saying you have never had a conflict
Escalating to the supervisor as the first step
A story that ends without resolution or learning

followUps.question: What if the other person still disagreed after the discussion?
followUps.answer: Agree on how to decide (a data point, a quick prototype, or the lead's call), escalate together with both options laid out fairly, then commit fully to the decision even if it was not yours: "disagree and commit".

followUps.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your supervisor or manager.
followUps.answer: Same path, more respectfully: bring data, propose instead of complain, accept their decision once heard, and show what happened. Example: suggesting automated tests for a flaky module, backed by the number of bugs it caused.

questions.title: Tell me about a time you failed or made a mistake
questions.prompt:
"Tell me about a time you failed." or "Tell me about a mistake you made and what you did about it."

Why do interviewers ask this, which story should you pick, and how do you tell it so that it builds trust instead of hurting you?
hints: They are testing ownership and learning, not looking for someone who never fails.
Pick a real mistake with real but limited impact, where you can show what you did next.
Own it fast -> limit the damage -> find the root cause -> prevent it from happening again -> share the lesson.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Picks a fake failure ("I failed to sleep because I worked too hard"), or blames others or circumstances, or tells a story with no fix and no lesson.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: A real mistake told with STAR: clear ownership early in the story, quick damage control, root-cause analysis, a concrete prevention step (process, test, automation), and a lesson that changed how you work.

solution.summary: Choose a real mistake with limited impact, own it plainly, then spend most of the answer on what you did: how fast you raised it, how you limited the damage, the root cause you found, the change you made so it cannot happen again, and what you learned.
solution.explanation:
### Why they ask
Everyone makes mistakes in production systems. Teams want people who **surface problems quickly** and **fix the system**, not people who hide errors. For banks and fintechs, this honesty matters even more.

### Picking the story
- **Real**: a genuine error you made, not a disguised strength.
- **Limited impact**: not a catastrophe that suggests poor judgement, not so trivial that nothing was at stake.
- **Yours**: you made it, you fixed it.
- **Resolved**: with a prevention step and a lesson.
Good sources: an internship bug, a missed deadline in a team project, a failed exam or contest you then prepared differently for, a deployment mistake.

### The response loop
1. **Own it fast**: tell the right person within minutes.
2. **Limit the damage**: roll back, inform the people affected.
3. **Root cause**: ask "why" until you reach something you can change.
4. **Prevent it**: a checklist, a test, an automated check.
5. **Share the lesson** so others benefit.

### Sample answer (the timeline walks through it)
> During my internship I deployed a configuration change to the shared staging server using a payment-gateway URL I had copied from an old wiki page. It was wrong, and for about 15 minutes every payment test the QA team ran failed. When I saw the errors, I checked my change and told my lead right away that it was probably mine, rolled it back, and confirmed the tests passed again. The root cause was the outdated wiki page and the fact that nothing validated config values before deployment. I fixed the page, and the next day I added a CI check that validates gateway URLs before any deploy. Since then I always verify config against the source of truth, and I try to make a mistake impossible to repeat, not just fix it once.

### Also prepared: a "failure" (not a mistake)
Example: not qualifying in a programming contest, then changing your preparation (topic-wise practice, timed mock contests) and the result next time.
keyPoints: A real mistake with limited impact, owned without excuses
Raise it fast and limit the damage
Root cause plus a concrete prevention step
A lesson that changed how you work

visuals.title: The mistake response loop

frames.note: What a strong answer demonstrates, in order. Interviewers listen especially for "Own it fast" and "Prevent it".

flowchart LR m["Mistake happens"] --> own["Own it fast
tell the lead within minutes"] own --> fix["Limit the damage
roll back, inform people"] fix --> rc["Find the root cause
not just the symptom"] rc --> prev["Prevent it

short note for the team"]

visuals.title: Example story: a bad config on staging
visuals.caption: Minutes from the deploy. The prevention step (a CI check) was merged the next day.

steps.note: **Minute 0.** During my internship I deployed a configuration change to the shared staging server. I had copied the payment-gateway sandbox URL from an old document, and it was wrong.
**Minutes 5-20.** Every payment test the QA team ran started failing. For 15 minutes they assumed it was their test data.

**Minute 20.** When I saw the errors in the team channel, I checked my change, realised it was mine, and **told my lead immediately**: "This is probably my config change, I'm rolling it back now." Owning it fast is the most important part of the story.
**Minutes 26-32.** I rolled back to the previous configuration, confirmed the payment tests passed again, and told QA they could continue.
**Minutes 32-42.** Root cause, not just symptom: the URL came from an outdated wiki page, and nothing validated config values before deploying.

**Prevention and lesson.** I wrote a short note for the team, fixed the wiki page, and the next day added a check to the CI pipeline that validates gateway URLs before deployment. Lesson: verify config against the source of truth, and make mistakes impossible to repeat, not just fixed once.

pitfalls: Choosing a fake failure that is really a strength
Blaming teammates, tools or the university
A story so severe it raises doubts about your judgement
No prevention step and no lesson

followUps.question: What would you do if you found a bug you introduced in production?
followUps.answer: Tell the team immediately, assess the impact, roll back or hotfix depending on severity, communicate to the affected people, then do a blameless root-cause review and add a test or check so it cannot recur.

followUps.question: Tell me about a time you received critical feedback.
followUps.answer: Describe the feedback without defensiveness, what you changed, and a later result that shows the change worked. Thank the person in the story; it shows you value feedback.

questions.title: Where do you see yourself in five years?
questions.prompt:
"Where do you see yourself in five years?"

What is the interviewer really checking, and how do you answer honestly if you are unsure, want to move into management or a specialisation, or are thinking about higher studies abroad?
hints: They want to know whether your goals fit what this job can offer, and whether you are likely to stay and grow.
Talk about skills and responsibilities you want to grow into, not job titles or salary.
Year 1: learn and deliver. Years 2-3: own something. Years 4-5: design and mentor. Connect it to this role.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "I want your job", "I will have my own startup", "I will be abroad doing a master's", or "I have not thought about it."

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: An ambitious but realistic growth path in skills and responsibility (deliver -> own -> design and mentor), aligned with what the company offers, honest without volunteering plans that make you look short-term.

solution.summary: Describe a realistic growth path in skills and responsibility: in year one, learn the systems and deliver reliably; in two to three years, own a module or service; by five years, design features and mentor juniors, and explain why this role is a good place to grow that way.
solution.explanation:
### What they are checking
1. **Ambition**: do you want to grow?
2. **Fit**: can this company offer the growth you want?
3. **Retention**: hiring and training a junior costs money; will you stay long enough?

### A strong structure (see the timeline)
- **Year 1**: learn the codebase, practices and domain; ship features reliably.
- **Years 2-3**: own a module or service end to end, review code, join on-call.
- **Years 4-5**: design features, make technical decisions, mentor juniors; possibly specialise (backend, mobile, data, security) or start leading a small team.
Then connect it: "This role is a good place for that because..."

### If you are unsure about the long term
That is normal. Talk about the direction (strong backend engineer, broad full-stack skills) rather than a title: *"I am still discovering whether I enjoy distributed systems or product engineering more, but either way I want to be the person the team trusts with hard problems."*

### If you are considering higher studies abroad
Many CSE graduates in Bangladesh think about a master's abroad, and interviewers know it. Do not lie, but do not lead with it either. Focus on the skills you want to build in this role. If they ask directly, answer honestly and positively: what you want to learn first, and that you are committed to contributing while you are there. A false promise damages trust far more.

### Avoid
- "I want your job" (sounds arrogant or like a cliché).
- Titles and salary as the main goal.
- Plans unrelated to the role (a different career, your own startup next year).
keyPoints: Growth in skills and responsibility, not titles or salary
Year 1 deliver -> years 2-3 own -> years 4-5 design and mentor
Connect your path to what this company offers
Honest without volunteering short-term plans

visuals.title: A five-year growth path
visuals.caption: Lanes are stages of your career; the axis is years in the role.

steps.note: **Year 1: learn and deliver.** *"In my first year I want to learn your systems and engineering practices well and become someone who ships features reliably with good tests."*
**Years 2-3: ownership.** *"After that I'd like to own a part of the system, say a service or module, end to end..."*
*"...and take part in code reviews and on-call, so I understand how things behave in production."*
**Years 4-5: wider impact.** *"In five years I see myself as a strong engineer who designs features, not just implements them..."*

*"...and helps new juniors the way seniors will have helped me."* Then tie it back: *"This role, with your mentoring culture and production scale, is a great place to build that."* Ambitious, realistic, and growth inside the company.

rows: "Leading the design of features and mentoring juniors."
"Building products end to end; I enjoy owning outcomes."
Focus on skills you will build here; answer honestly if asked directly
"I'm still choosing a specialisation, but I want to be trusted with hard problems."
Talk about responsibility and impact; salary follows

pitfalls: Naming a title or salary as the main goal
Saying you will be somewhere else (another company, abroad, your startup) as the first thing
Having no answer at all
Promising things you do not intend (for example, staying "forever")

followUps.question: Do you want to go into management?
followUps.answer: Answer honestly; for a junior, the safe and genuine answer is usually "I want to become a strong engineer first; later I will see whether I enjoy leading people or going deeper technically, and I like that both paths exist here" (if they do).

followUps.question: How long do you plan to stay with us?
followUps.answer: Do not promise a number you cannot keep. Say you are looking for a place to grow for the long term, and that as long as you are learning and contributing, you see no reason to leave.

questions.title: How do you handle pressure and tight deadlines?
questions.prompt:
"How do you work under pressure?" or "Tell me about a time you had a tight deadline."

What does a convincing answer show beyond "I stay calm and work hard", and what does a good example from a student project or internship look like?
hints: "I work late" is not a strategy. What do you do *before* working late?
Prioritise (must / should / could), protect focus time, and ask for help when blocked.
The key behaviour: tell people early, with options, when the plan is at risk.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "I work well under pressure; I just stay calm and work overnight until it is done." No method, a burnout signal, and no communication.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: A STAR story showing a method: break down and prioritise, focus on must-haves, detect risk early, communicate options to the lead, cut or defer scope deliberately, deliver what was promised, and reflect on what to do differently.

solution.summary: I stay calm by having a method: I break the work down and prioritise what must be delivered, protect focus time for it, ask for help quickly when blocked, and when the deadline is at risk I tell my lead early with options, so we cut or defer scope deliberately instead of missing the deadline by surprise.
solution.explanation:
### The method behind the calm
1. **Break down and estimate** the work.
2. **Prioritise** with MoSCoW: Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time).
3. **Do the must-haves first**, in focused blocks.
4. **Unblock fast**: if stuck for about an hour, ask with what you tried.
5. **Communicate early, with options**, as soon as a deadline looks at risk.
6. **Cut or defer scope deliberately**, agreed with the lead, rather than lowering quality everywhere.
7. **Reflect** afterwards: what would prevent this next time?

### Sample STAR answer (the visual follows the same week)
> **Situation**: In my internship we had a client demo on Friday for a transaction export feature.
> **Task**: I owned the feature: CSV export, date filters, PDF export and emailing the report.
> **Action**: On Monday I ranked the parts: CSV and filters were must-haves, PDF should, email could wait. On Wednesday morning I found that our PDF library rendered Bangla text incorrectly and fixing it would take two more days. That afternoon I told my lead, with two options: demo CSV and filters on Friday and deliver PDF on Tuesday, or rush everything. We chose the first, and email moved to the next sprint. I spent Thursday finishing filters with tests.
> **Result**: The demo went smoothly with exactly what we promised, PDF shipped on Tuesday, and the client was happy because nothing was a surprise. I learned that early communication is worth more than overtime.

### Variations to prepare
- **Exam week + project deadline** (student): planning, splitting the work with teammates, starting early.
- **Production issue** (internship): stay calm, follow the runbook, communicate status regularly.

### Avoid
Glorifying all-nighters, saying you never feel pressure, or stories where you missed the deadline without warning anyone.
keyPoints: Break down and prioritise: must, should, could
Focus on must-haves; ask for help quickly when blocked
Flag risk early, with options, to the lead
Cut or defer scope deliberately; keep quality on what ships
Reflect and improve the process

visuals.caption: Example from an internship: transaction export for a Friday client demo.

followUps.question: What do you do when two people give you urgent tasks at the same time?
followUps.answer: Do not guess: make the conflict visible, explain the effort for each, and ask the person who sets priorities (usually the lead) to decide. Then tell both requesters what will happen when.

followUps.question: How do you avoid burnout?
followUps.answer: Sustainable pace: realistic estimates, early communication instead of overtime, focus blocks, and real breaks. Occasional crunch happens, but it should be the exception, not the plan.

questions.title: What questions should you ask the interviewer?
questions.prompt:
At the end of almost every round you will hear: *"Do you have any questions for us?"*

Why does this matter, which questions leave a good impression (and which do not), and how should the questions differ for an engineer, a manager and HR?
hints: "No, I think you covered everything" is a missed opportunity.
Ask about the work, the team, how people grow, and next steps, tailored to who is in front of you.
Prepare 5, ask 2-3, and ideally refer to something said earlier in the interview.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "No questions." Or questions whose answers are on the careers page, or only about leave, salary and promotions in the first technical round.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Two or three thoughtful, prepared questions matched to the interviewer's role, about the team's work, expectations for a new joiner, how quality is ensured and how juniors grow, plus a question about next steps.

solution.summary: Always ask two or three prepared questions tailored to the person: ask engineers about the work and how the team builds software, managers about expectations and growth, and HR about the process and next steps. It shows genuine interest and helps you decide whether you want the job.
solution.explanation:
### Why it matters
- It signals **interest and preparation**, and it is often the last impression you leave.
- It is **your** interview too: you learn whether the team will help you grow.
- A question that refers to something said earlier shows you were listening.

### Questions that work well
**About the role**
- "What would a new junior engineer typically work on in the first three months?"
- "What does success look like for this role after six months?"

**About the team and engineering**
- "How does the team review code and test changes before release?"
- "How is work planned: sprints, Kanban, something else?"
- "What is the biggest technical challenge the team is facing right now?"

**About growth**
- "How are juniors mentored or onboarded?"
- "Is there time or budget for learning, such as courses or conferences?"

**About next steps**
- "What are the next steps in the process, and when can I expect to hear back?"

### Tailor to the person (see the comparison)
Engineers can tell you about daily work; managers about expectations; HR about process, policies and benefits.

### Questions to avoid (or to time well)
- Anything answered on the first page of their website.
- Salary, leave and benefits in an early technical round (save them for HR or the offer stage, unless they raise it).
- "How soon can I be promoted?" in the first interview.
- Negative framing: "Is your company going to have layoffs?" (if you need to know, ask about stability more neutrally later).

### Practical tips
Write your questions down and bring them; it is fine to look at your notes. If all your questions were answered, say so and mention one: "You already explained how code review works, which was my main question. Could you tell me more about how the team handles production incidents?"
keyPoints: Always ask two or three questions; prepare about five
Tailor them to the interviewer's role
Ask about the work, quality practices, growth and next steps
Avoid questions answered on the website and premature salary/leave questions

questions.title: What are your salary expectations?
questions.prompt:
"What are your salary expectations?" or "How much are you expecting?"

How do you research a fair range as a fresh graduate (in Bangladesh or for remote roles), when should you give a number, how do you state a range, and how do you negotiate politely once an offer arrives?
hints: Never answer with a number you invented on the spot. Where would you find real data?
Know three numbers before the call: your walk-away, your target and your stretch.
Ask for their budgeted range first if you can; if pressed, give a researched range whose bottom is near your target, and discuss the total package, not only the base.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Says "anything is fine", or names a random number, or a figure far above the market, then accepts the first offer without asking what is included.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Has researched the market for this role, company type and city, knows walk-away/target/stretch, tries to learn their range first, gives a range anchored at the target, asks about the whole package, negotiates politely with reasons, and gets the final terms in writing.

solution.summary: Research the market range for this role and company type, decide your walk-away, target and stretch numbers, try to learn the company's budget first, and if asked, give a range whose lower end is close to your target, saying it depends on the total package. At the offer stage, negotiate politely with reasons and get the final terms in writing.
solution.explanation:
### 1. Research before the call
Salaries vary widely in Bangladesh by company type (local product company, software service company, multinational, bank, startup), city, and the role's stack. Sources:
- **Seniors, alumni and friends** working at similar companies (the most reliable source for freshers).
- **Job postings** that show a salary range (some local job boards and company posts include one).
- **Developer communities** and online salary surveys, used carefully (small samples, often self-reported).
- For international or remote roles, sites such as Glassdoor or Levels.fyi, adjusted for the role's location and level.
Write down a range for *this* kind of company, not the highest number you heard.

### 2. Know your three numbers
- **Walk-away**: the minimum you would accept (cost of living, other offers).
- **Target**: a fair market number for you.
- **Stretch**: the top of a realistic range.

### 3. If they ask early (screening call)
Try to learn their range first:
> "I'm still learning about the role. Could you share the budgeted range for this position?"
If they insist, give a **range** based on research, not a single number, with the bottom near your target, and leave room:
> "Based on my research for junior backend roles at similar companies, I'm looking at roughly X to Y, depending on the total package."
Many application forms (including on local job sites) ask for an "expected salary" field: fill it with your researched number or range, not a random guess.

### 4. At the offer stage: look at the whole package
Ask what the figure includes (see the checklist visual): gross vs take-home, festival bonuses, provident fund, increments, probation, insurance, other benefits, any service bond.

### 5. Negotiate politely
- Start with appreciation and enthusiasm.
- Ask, with a reason: "Is there flexibility on the base? Based on my research and the internship experience I bring, I was hoping for closer to X."
- If the base is fixed, ask about other levers: the first review after probation, a joining bonus, a learning budget.
- Never invent competing offers. If you have a real one, mention it factually.
- Get the final agreement **in writing** (offer letter).

### Tone
Negotiation is normal and expected; doing it respectfully does not cost you the offer at reasonable companies. Freshers usually have less leverage, so focus on a fair base, a clear review date, and learning opportunities.
keyPoints: Research a market range for this role and company type; know walk-away, target and stretch
Try to learn their budget first; if pressed, give a range anchored at your target
Evaluate the total package, not only the base
Negotiate politely with reasons; never invent offers
Get the final terms in writing

followUps.question: What is your current salary?
followUps.answer: For a fresh graduate, you can say this is your first full-time role and share your internship stipend only if relevant. If you are employed, it is reasonable to focus on your expectation for this role based on market research rather than your current figure.

followUps.question: What if they say the offer is final?
followUps.answer: Thank them, then decide calmly: compare the total package with your walk-away number and the learning opportunity. You can still ask for non-salary items, such as an early review or a learning budget, and ask for a day or two to decide.

questions.title: How to approach a coding interview (thinking aloud)
questions.prompt:
You are given a coding problem in a live interview (on a whiteboard, a shared editor or a call). What exactly do you do from the moment you read the problem until time runs out?

Describe the steps (clarify -> examples -> brute force -> optimise -> code -> test), how you **think aloud**, how you manage time, and what to do when you get stuck.
hints: Interviewers grade the process as much as the final code. What can they see if you code in silence?
Never start coding before you have clarified the problem, worked an example, and agreed on an approach.
Clarify -> examples -> brute force with complexity -> optimise -> confirm -> code while narrating -> dry-run and edge cases -> complexity.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Reads the problem, goes silent, starts coding immediately, gets stuck on an edge case at minute 30, and says "I think it works" without testing.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Clarifies constraints and edge cases, works examples, states a brute force with its complexity, improves it and confirms the plan, codes cleanly while narrating, dry-runs the code on an example and edge cases, and states the final complexity, asking for a hint after a few minutes of being stuck.

solution.summary: I follow a fixed routine and think aloud throughout: clarify the problem and constraints, work through examples, state a brute-force solution with its complexity, optimise it and confirm the approach with the interviewer, code it while narrating, then test it by dry-running examples and edge cases and finish with the time and space complexity.
solution.explanation:
### What interviewers score
1. **Problem solving**: can you get from a vague problem to a working approach?
2. **Communication**: can they follow your thinking?
3. **Coding**: is the code correct, clean and readable?
4. **Testing**: do you verify your own work?
Silence hides 1, 2 and 4. That is why thinking aloud matters.

### The routine (the visuals show the time plan and a full example)
1. **Clarify**: restate the problem; ask about input size, value ranges, duplicates, negatives, empty input, what to return when there is no answer.
2. **Examples**: one normal, one tricky; check your understanding.
3. **Brute force**: state it with its complexity. Use the constraints: n up to 10^5 means O(n²) (about 10^10 steps) is too slow; aim for O(n log n) or O(n).
4. **Optimise**: find the repeated or wasted work; think through common patterns (hash map, two pointers, sliding window, sorting, binary search, heap, BFS/DFS, DP). **Confirm** the plan before coding.
5. **Code**: meaningful names, small helper functions, narrate the important lines.
6. **Test**: dry-run line by line with real values, then edge cases. Fix bugs calmly; finding your own bug is a positive signal.
7. **Wrap up**: time and space complexity, trade-offs, what you would improve.

### When you are stuck
- Say what you are thinking: "I know I need to find pairs faster than O(n²)..."
- Go back to a small example and solve it by hand, watching what you do.
- After 3-5 minutes without progress, **ask for a hint**, explaining what you tried. Taking a hint well is better than freezing.

### Online assessments (no interviewer)
The same routine, silently: read constraints first, solve the easiest question first, test with your own edge cases before submitting, and watch the time per question.

### Practice the habit
Practise problems out loud, with a timer, ideally with a friend acting as interviewer. Record yourself once; it is uncomfortable but very effective.

code.code:
def two_sum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
    seen = {}  # value -> index of numbers already passed
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - x
        if need in seen:
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []


# Test out loud: normal case, duplicates, negatives, no answer
print(two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9))  # [0, 1]
print(two_sum([3, 3], 6))  # [0, 1]
print(two_sum([-4, 1, 9], 5))  # [0, 2]
print(two_sum([1, 2], 7))  # []

keyPoints: Clarify inputs, outputs, constraints and edge cases before coding
Brute force with complexity first, then optimise and confirm the plan
Think aloud while coding; keep the code clean
Test by dry-running examples and edge cases; state final complexity
Ask for a hint after a few minutes stuck, explaining what you tried

visuals.title: Time plan for a 45-minute coding round
visuals.caption: One lane per phase; labels are the minutes. Real interviews vary, but the order rarely does.

steps.note: **Clarify (about 4 min).** Restate the problem and ask about inputs, outputs, constraints and edge cases before writing anything.
**Examples (about 3 min).** Work one normal and one tricky example by hand; it often reveals the pattern.
**Brute force (about 3 min).** Say the simplest correct idea and its complexity, even if you will not code it.
**Optimize (about 7 min).** Find the bottleneck in the brute force and pick a better approach; confirm the plan with the interviewer.
**Code (about 15 min).** Write clean, readable code while narrating what each part does.
**Test (about 8 min).** Dry-run your code on the example, then edge cases; fix bugs calmly.
**Wrap up (about 5 min).** State time and space complexity and mention possible improvements or trade-offs.

visuals.title: One problem, start to finish, out loud (Two Sum)
visuals.caption: The note is what you say; the panels are what you write down. Code lines refer to the JavaScript solution.

steps.note: **Clarify.** Problem: "Given an array and a target, find two numbers that add up to the target." You say: *"Should I return the indices or the values? Is there always exactly one answer? Can numbers be negative or repeated? How large can the array be?"*
**Examples.** *"Let me check my understanding: for [2, 7, 11, 15] and target 9 the answer is [0, 1]. A tricky one: [3, 3] with target 6 must return [0, 1], so I can't use the same element twice."*
**Brute force.** *"The simplest correct approach checks every pair: O(n²) time, O(1) space. With n up to 100,000 that is about 10^10 operations, too slow, so I'd like to optimise before coding."*

**Optimise and agree.** *"For each number x I need target − x. If I store the numbers I have already seen in a hash map from value to index, I can check that in O(1). That gives O(n) time and O(n) space. Does that sound good before I code it?"*

panels.title: whiteboard notes
items: map value -> index: O(n) time, O(n) space

steps.note: **Code, narrating.** *"I loop once. For each index I compute need; if need is already in the map I return both indices, otherwise I store the current value. Checking before inserting means I never pair an element with itself."*

panels.title: whiteboard notes
items: map value -> index: O(n) time, O(n) space

steps.note: **Test by dry-running.** *"For [2, 7, 11, 15]: i = 0, need 7, not seen, store 2. i = 1, need 2, found at index 0, return [0, 1]."* Walk the code line by line with real values, out loud.

panels.title: whiteboard notes
items: map value -> index: O(n) time, O(n) space

steps.note: **Edge cases.** Duplicates [3, 3] -> [0, 1]; negatives [-4, 1, 9] with target 5 -> [0, 2]; no answer [1, 2] with target 7 -> [] (agreed during clarification). All pass.

panels.title: whiteboard notes
items: map value -> index: O(n) time, O(n) space

steps.note: **Wrap up.** *"Time O(n), one pass with O(1) average map operations; space O(n) for the map. If the array were sorted, two pointers would give O(1) extra space."* Every step was visible to the interviewer: that is what they grade.

followUps.question: What if you cannot find the optimal solution?
followUps.answer: Implement the best correct solution you have (a clean brute force beats broken optimal code), state its complexity honestly, and explain what you would try next. Partial credit for a working, well-tested solution is real.

followUps.question: Which language should you use?
followUps.answer: The one you are fastest and most accurate in, usually the one you used for problem solving (C++, Java, Python or JavaScript). Know its standard library for maps, sets, sorting, heaps and queues well.

quiz.question: In the STAR method, what do the letters stand for?
options: Strategy, Timeline, Analysis, Review
Situation, Teamwork, Approach, Reflection
Situation, Task, Action, Result
Skills, Talent, Attitude, Reliability
quiz.explanation: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result: a structure for "Tell me about a time..." answers that keeps them concrete and short.

quiz.question: Which part of a STAR answer should take the most time?
options: Situation
Action
Task
Result
quiz.explanation: The interviewer is scoring what you did and why, so Action should be roughly half the answer. Long situations are the most common mistake.

quiz.question: What is the best structure for "Tell me about yourself" as a fresh graduate?
options: Present -> past -> future, tailored to the role, in 60-90 seconds
Your CV in order: education, CGPA, courses, projects, then skills
A chronological story from school to graduation, so they see your background
Two or three sentences, so the interviewer can move on to technical questions
quiz.explanation: Present-past-future gives a short, relevant pitch with proof points and a link to the role. A CV recital or a life story is long and unfocused (they already have your CV), and two or three sentences waste the chance to steer the interview towards your strongest material.

quiz.question: Which weakness answer is the strongest?
options: "I'm a perfectionist, so I sometimes spend too long polishing my work."
"I don't have a major weakness that affects my work."
"I find teamwork hard, so I prefer to take tasks I can do on my own."
"I used to underestimate tasks; now I split work into pieces under a day and track estimate vs actual."
quiz.explanation: It is real, not core to the job, and shows a concrete improvement system. The perfectionist line is a cliché, "no weaknesses" shows low self-awareness, and avoiding teamwork is disqualifying for most roles.

quiz.question: Early in a screening call the recruiter asks for your salary expectation, before you know much about the role. What is the best first response?
options: Ask whether they can share the budgeted range for the role
Say "anything is fine", since a fresher should not negotiate
Name the highest figure you have heard from a friend, to leave room to come down
Decline to discuss salary at all until you have a written offer
quiz.explanation: Asking for their range first gives you information without weakening your position; if they insist, give a researched range. "Anything is fine" invites a low offer, an unresearched number can price you out or undersell you, and refusing to discuss it at all can come across as evasive.

quiz.question: If you must give a salary range, where should your real target sit?
options: At the top of the range
Exactly in the middle of the range
At or near the bottom of the range
Above the range, so the numbers you say sound modest
quiz.explanation: Employers tend to anchor on the lower end of a range, so its bottom should be a number you would be happy with. With the target at the top or in the middle, the likely offer lands below it; a target above the whole range means you are underselling yourself from the start.

quiz.question: At the end of a technical round with an engineer, which question leaves the best impression?
options: How many days of annual leave will I get?
How soon can someone in this role be promoted?
No questions, you covered everything clearly.
What would a new junior typically work on in the first three months?
quiz.explanation: It shows interest in the actual work and is something an engineer can answer. Leave and promotion questions fit better with HR later; having no questions is a missed opportunity.

quiz.question: In a coding interview, what should you do right after reading the problem?
options: Start coding the brute force right away so you have something working
Restate it and clarify inputs, outputs, constraints and edge cases
Ask for a hint so you do not waste time going in the wrong direction
Write the function signature and a full set of unit tests first
quiz.explanation: Clarifying first prevents solving the wrong problem and shows structured thinking. Coding before agreeing on an approach is the classic mistake, hints are for when you are stuck after trying, and testing comes after you have code.

quiz.question: n can be up to 100,000 and your first idea is O(n²). What should you do?
options: Say it is about 10^10 steps, too slow, and look for an O(n log n) or O(n) approach before coding
Code it anyway, since a working O(n²) solution is all the interviewer needs to see
Stay quiet while you search for a faster idea, so you do not reveal a weak approach
Ask the interviewer to lower the limit on n so that the O(n²) idea will pass
quiz.explanation: Stating the brute force and why it is too slow, out loud, shows you use the constraints to guide the design; then optimise and confirm the plan before coding. Silence hides exactly the reasoning the interviewer is grading, and the constraints are part of the problem, not something to negotiate away.

quiz.question: In a "conflict with a teammate" story, which is a red flag?
options: Talking to the teammate privately first
Agreeing on the shared goal before choosing an option
Committing to the final decision even though it was not yours
Proving you were right and reporting them to the supervisor
quiz.explanation: Blame and escalating first suggest you are hard to work with. The other three are exactly the behaviours interviewers want to hear.

quiz.question: Which story best answers "Tell me about a time you failed or made a mistake"?
options: "I worked so hard on our final-year project that I forgot to rest and burned out before the demo."
"I deployed a wrong config to staging; I flagged it within minutes, rolled back, and added a CI check so it cannot happen again."
"A teammate broke the build before our demo, and I stayed up all night to fix it for the team."
"I have never really failed, because I always plan carefully and double-check my work."
quiz.explanation: It is a real mistake of your own, with fast ownership, a fix, prevention and a lesson. The others are a disguised strength, someone else's mistake, or a lack of self-awareness.

quiz.question: You plan to apply for a master's abroad in about two years. Asked "Where do you see yourself in five years?", what is the best approach?
options: Lead with your plan to leave for a master's in two years, so they hear it from you first
